issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s clear and unequivocal repudiation of the landlord’s title may constitute an act injurious to the landlord’s interest and a ground for eviction.
material_facts: The landlord’s plaint identified a registered sale deed by which she had purchased the building from the tenant’s earlier landlord.
The tenant denied the landlord’s title and the genuineness of the sale deed in his written statement, denied her title in evidence, and stated that he did not accept her as his landlady.
Documents relating to the landlord’s ownership were on record, but the tenant continued to refuse to acknowledge her title.
The tenant’s conduct was not merely a bona fide request that the landlord prove ownership while the tenant maintained his status as tenant.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s denial of the landlord’s title was a ground for eviction under Section 12(1)(c) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961, and the eviction decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(c) of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961 covers denial of the landlord’s title or disclaimer of tenancy when the tenant renounces the character of tenant and clearly and unequivocally asserts title in himself or a third party; a bona fide request for proof of ownership without disowning the tenancy is not enough. This applies the principle in Section 111(g) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and the rule stated in Devasahayam v. P. Savithramma, drawing on Sheela v. Prahlad Rai Prem Prakash. Majati Subbarao v. P.V.K. Krishnarao establishes that denial need not precede the eviction proceeding. Section 116 of the Evidence Act and Bhagadi Kannababu v. Vuggina Pydamma support the landlord-tenant estoppel principle.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant in a proceeding governed by rent-control legislation.
predicates.tenant_categorically_rejects_landlord_ti: The tenant unequivocally refuses to acknowledge the claimant as landlord, rather than merely asking for proof of ownership while accepting the tenancy.
predicates.tenant_persists_after_ownership_document: The tenant continues to reject the claimant’s title despite ownership documents being available in the proceeding.
predicates.tenant_claims_title_for_self_or_another: The tenant clearly asserts that title belongs to the tenant or to someone other than the landlord.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction case involves a tenant’s categorical rejection of the landlord’s title, accompanied by persistence despite ownership documents or a clear claim of title for someone else, the denial is a ground for eviction.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court in a second appeal may not set aside concurrent factual findings unless those findings are perverse.
material_facts: The trial court found that the tenant had denied the landlord’s title and granted eviction on that ground.
The first appellate court affirmed that finding and decree.
The High Court set aside the concurrent finding and eviction decree, although the Supreme Court found no perversity in the lower courts’ factual finding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to disturb the concurrent finding, and its judgment was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Concurrent findings of fact should not be disturbed in a second appeal unless perverse. The Court relied on Deep Chandra Juneja v. Lajwanti Kathuria, Yash Pal v. Ram Lal, and Firojuddin v. Babu Singh.

rule.if: second_appeal_case and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_not_perverse and high_court_sets_findings_aside

predicates.second_appeal_case: The matter before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual finding.
predicates.findings_not_perverse: The concurrent factual finding is not shown to be perverse.
predicates.high_court_sets_findings_aside: The High Court reverses or sets aside the concurrent factual finding.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, if the lower courts made the same non-perverse factual finding and the High Court sets it aside, that interference is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: A title question considered in an ordinary eviction proceeding is generally considered only incidentally and is not finally determined there.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the landlord’s ownership could be examined in the eviction proceeding.
The eviction proceeding did not frame an issue of title.
The Court distinguished an exceptional earlier case in which title had been directly and substantially in issue and the finding was held to operate as res judicata.
issues.conclusion: The eviction proceeding could consider title incidentally, but it could not finally determine title in the ordinary circumstances of this case; the exceptional res judicata case did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Bhagadi Kannababu v. Vuggina Pydamma, relying on Tej Bhan Madan v. II Additional District Judge, states that an eviction court determines whether the landlord-tenant relationship exists; title may be considered incidentally but is not finally decided. Mohd. Nooman v. Mohd. Jabed Alam was expressly confined to exceptional facts where title was directly and substantially in issue, so its res judicata result does not ordinarily apply. Section 116 of the Evidence Act supports the estoppel principle between landlord and tenant.

predicates.ordinary_eviction_proceeding: A court is deciding a proceeding for eviction rather than a suit principally seeking a final determination of title.
predicates.title_considered_incidentally: The court examines title only as part of deciding the issues necessary to the eviction proceeding.
predicates.title_not_directly_and_substantially_in_: The parties have not made title a directly and substantially framed issue for decision.

issues.definition: When an ordinary eviction proceeding considers title only incidentally and title is not directly and substantially in issue, the title finding is not finally binding.
